results.summary_before: This design is a 4-bit ALU inspired by the Supercon.6 badge, implemented as a finite state machine with combinational logic in Verilog. It takes two 4-bit data inputs and a control signal, and produces a 4-bit result along with a carry-out. The design is tested using cocotb, a Python-based verification framework. No external hardware is required.

results.summary_before: This design reads an incremental rotary encoder and displays the resulting count on a seven-segment display. It samples the encoder pins every clock cycle, detects rising edges on pin A, and increments or decrements a 4-bit counter based on the state of pin B, with a debounce period of 125 clock cycles. The design requires an external rotary encoder connected to pins A and B. After reset, turning the encoder updates the displayed count.

results.summary_before: This design implements a 6-bit Gray code counter in the Amaranth HDL. It outputs a sequence where only one bit changes between successive counts, which can help reduce switching noise in certain applications. The counter is controlled by external clock and reset signals and requires no additional hardware. The project serves as a simple educational example of Gray code and Amaranth-based design.

results.summary_before: This design implements a 1-bit ALU from Tanenbaum's book, supporting AND, NOT, OR, and ADD operations selected by two mode inputs. It includes enable and invert controls for the inputs and a carry-in for addition, and the output is shown on a 7-segment display with the carry-out on the decimal point. The design is intended for educational use and can be chained to create wider ALUs. No external hardware is needed beyond the on-board display.

results.summary_before: This design combines two independent circuits: a Fibonacci sequence calculator using 56-bit integers and a Gold code generator for CCSDS X-band PN Delta-DOR. The Fibonacci terms are displayed one hex character at a time on the 7-segment display, with the decimal point marking the least significant bit. The Gold code generator uses LFSRs and allows parallel loading of 6 bits to select different sequences; the display dot shows either the Fibonacci output or the Gold code output based on an input select. The design is tested manually by driving the clock and setting the appropriate inputs; no external hardware is required.
